title: gcd and lcm from Prime Factorizations
short: Take the smaller exponent of each prime for the gcd and the larger for the lcm; then gcd(a, b) · lcm(a, b) = ab.
trouble: Students take the larger exponents for the gcd, or expect gcd · lcm to equal the product for three numbers too (for 2, 2 and 2 it gives 4, not 8).

blocks.html: Once numbers are written as products of primes (thanks to unique factorization), their gcd and lcm can be read off directly, and a tidy identity connects the two.

Write $a$ and $b$ using the same list of primes, allowing exponent $0$: $a = \prod p^{\alpha_p}$ and $b = \prod p^{\beta_p}$. Then $$\gcd(a, b) = \prod p^{\min(\alpha_p, \beta_p)}, \qquad \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) = \prod p^{\max(\alpha_p, \beta_p)}.$$

By unique factorization, $d \mid a$ exactly when $d$ uses only the primes of $a$, each with an exponent at most $\alpha_p$. So a common divisor can use each prime at most $\min(\alpha_p, \beta_p)$ times, and the greatest one uses exactly that many. A common multiple must contain each number completely, so it needs at least $\max(\alpha_p, \beta_p)$ copies of each prime, and the least one uses exactly that many. Since $\min(\alpha, \beta) + \max(\alpha, \beta) = \alpha + \beta$ for every prime, $$\gcd(a, b) \cdot \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) = ab.$$

blocks.cap: Exponents of each prime in the first example.

blocks.title: Reading off gcd and lcm
blocks.q: Find $\gcd(a, b)$ and $\operatorname{lcm}(a, b)$ for $a = 2^{3} \cdot 3^{2} \cdot 5 = 360$ and $b = 2 \cdot 3^{4} \cdot 7 = 1134$.

blocks.title: Working backward
blocks.q: Two positive integers have gcd $12$ and lcm $360$. One of them is $72$. What is the other?

blocks.title: Three numbers
steps: Here $2 \cdot 180 = 360$, but $12 \cdot 18 \cdot 20 = 4320$: the product rule is only for two numbers.

blocks.html: Taking the larger exponents for the gcd (that gives the lcm), or using $\gcd \cdot \operatorname{lcm} = \text{product}$ for three numbers. For $2, 2, 2$: the gcd and lcm are both $2$, so their product is $4$, not $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8$. With three numbers, min plus max misses the middle exponent.

Two special cases are worth remembering. Numbers are coprime exactly when they share no prime at all; then every minimum is $0$, so $\gcd(a, b) = 1$ and $\operatorname{lcm}(a, b) = ab$. And when $a \mid b$, every exponent of $a$ is at most the matching exponent of $b$, so $\gcd(a, b) = a$ and $\operatorname{lcm}(a, b) = b$. The lcm answers "when do two cycles line up again?": lights blinking every $12$ and every $18$ seconds blink together every $\operatorname{lcm}(12, 18) = 36$ seconds.
For large numbers, factoring is slow, while the Euclidean algorithm is fast. So computers find the gcd by Euclid and then the lcm as $ab / \gcd(a, b)$.
gcd: the smaller exponent of each prime. lcm: the larger. For two numbers, $\gcd(a, b) \cdot \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) = ab$.
